We thank the reviewer for their valuable feedback. We address your comments in the following.

---

**Q1**: The reward signal is fully determined by the teacher model’s likelihood estimates. If the teacher is miscalibrated or biased, the shaping signal may misrepresent information gain. No calibration analysis or correction mechanism is discussed.

**A1**: This is a very important point that must be tackled when implementing our potential function for PBRS. On one hand, we want to keep the potential signal stationary for training stability. On the other hand, we want to ensure that the potential function doesn’t become stale, or miscalibrated in your words. Our main method to prevent staleness is refreshing the teacher model from the latest policy checkpoint every n iterations. Our experiments in Section 4.3 show that your concern is valid; if we do not refresh the teacher, the biased potential causes the reward curve to collapse. However, when we do refresh the teacher, reward continues to climb. We have updated the manuscript to discuss the relationship between teacher calibration and refreshing the teacher ([screenshot](https://imgur.com/a/zhkOgyn)).

---

**Q2**: All experiments use the same teacher model (Qwen-2.5), differing only in whether it is fixed or periodically refreshed. The paper does not evaluate how the reward behaves with different teachers, leaving the robustness of TIPS to teacher variation untested.

**A2**: Thank you for pointing this out. TIPS was designed with the intention of using the same model as the policy for the teacher. The teacher is simply a frozen checkpoint of the policy model being trained, refreshed at a fixed interval. Because the teacher and policy distributions are similar, the probability the teacher assigns to generating an answer may act as a **potential**, with which we can assign intermediate credit to the policy. However, we agree that exploring the use of other models as teachers is worthwhile. Our ablations yield the following results:

| Policy/Teacher | Frozen policy | Qwen3-4B-TIPS | Llama3.1-8B |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen2.5-7B  | 41.7  (+11.9%) | 30   (-19.5%) | 29  (-22.2%) |
| Qwen3-4B   | 48.4  (+7.3%) | 45.88 (+1.7%) | 43  (-4.7%) |

We see that using a frozen policy consistently performs best. Notably, it outperforms using a *stronger model* as a teacher. This supports our hypothesis that the similarity between the policy and teacher matters much more than the teacher’s strength.

We have added these results and a brief discussion of teacher selection to Section 4.3 ([screenshot](https://imgur.com/a/6rclzlc)).

--------

**Q3**: The need to query the teacher model for every reasoning turn increases training cost compared to standard PPO/GRPO. The paper does not quantify the additional compute or discuss trade-offs between stability and efficiency.

**A3**: We agree that this is a crucial point that we neglected to analyze. We have updated the manuscript with a report of the computational overhead of TIPS over the baselines, and a thorough analysis in Appendix H. 

When we compute the increase in FLOPs attributed to the teacher forward passes, we find a modest overhead of ~12% compared to PPO. To put this in context, GRPO requires 3.5x more FLOPs than PPO. 

Comparing runtime between TIPS and baselines is more challenging. Since rollout generation is the slowest phase of online LLM RL, the per-step runtime is mostly determined by the policy’s average response length. To get an estimate, however, we can compute (step time with reward)/(step time without reward). This yields an overhead of 16-17%. 

| Model | Without Reward (s/step) | With Reward (s/step) | Overhead (%) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen2.5-3B | 30.56 | 35.95 | 17.64 |
| Qwen2.5-7B | 93.00 | 108.22 | 16.37 |

Although the overhead is real, it is quite modest, and we believe the improvement in performance and stability is well worth this cost.

**Q3:** The entire framework's success hinges on the availability and quality of a "teacher model". The paper shows that this teacher must be "refreshed" periodically to prevent the potential function from becoming stale, which itself causes instability. This introduces new complexities, such as determining the optimal refresh rate.

**A3:** TIPS was designed with the intention of using the same model as the policy for the teacher. The teacher is simply a frozen checkpoint of the policy model being trained, refreshed at a fixed interval. Therefore, **the teacher model is always available.** We disagree that refreshing the teacher causes instability; our ablation in Fig. 6 shows that refreshing the teacher **prevents instability** associated with a stale potential function. However, we agree that choosing a good refresh rate is important for practitioners.

To this end, we ablate \(N $\in$ \{1, 100, 200, 250, 500\}\) for Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3-4B. We find that **performance is not extremely sensitive to N**. Very rare refreshes (N=500, effectively no refresh) lead to lower EM, while there is a broad optimum around N≈200; across all moderate intervals (100–500), TIPS outperforms PPO. We have added this ablation and a short discussion in Sec 4.3 of the revised manuscript. [Screenshots of refresh interval](https://imgur.com/a/62Q4nJ2)

---
**Q4:** As noted by the authors, the method is currently demonstrated only within the PPO framework. It is unclear how this segment-level PBRS approach would be integrated with other, potentially more sample-efficient, RL algorithms (e.g., off-policy methods).

**A4**: Thank you for pointing this out. Our current experiments are indeed instantiated within a PPO-style actor–critic framework, and we have clarified this scope in the revision.

Conceptually, TIPS is a segment-level potential-based reward shaping scheme: it only modifies how token-level returns are computed, via $ r'_t = r_t + \gamma \Phi(s*{t+1}) - \Phi(s_t)$ , and leaves the underlying policy update rule unchanged. Any RL algorithm that operates on return-to-go or advantages (e.g., other on-policy actor–critic methods like SAC) can in principle, use these shaped rewards, and the PBRS result guarantees that the optimal policy under the original outcome reward is preserved.

In the LLM RLVR setting we study, however, PPO/GRPO-type on-policy methods are currently the dominant and most stable choices; to allow clean, apples-to-apples comparisons, we focused our empirical evaluation on this family. Extending TIPS to dedicated off-policy algorithms for long-horizon LLM training is an interesting direction, but we view it as orthogonal and leave it for future work.

---
We believe that our response and additional experiment results address your concerns. However, please do not hesitate to let us know if you have any additional comments.

**Q3**: Theoretical Guarantees and Teacher Refresh: The policy invariance proof holds for a fixed potential function. Your refresh@200 strategy, while empirically beneficial, technically breaks this strict invariance between refresh windows. Can you comment on the theoretical implications of this? Did you observe any instability or "jumps" in the return values immediately after a refresh, and how does this relate to the "constant shift" mentioned in the text?

**A3**: Our formal proof indeed assumes a fixed potential $\Phi$, and we now clarify how this interacts with teacher refresh.

From a theoretical perspective:
For any **given rollout**, the teacher (and thus  $\Phi$) is **frozen**, and no gradients flow through $\Phi$. For that trajectory, the shaped return for token (t) in turn (k) can be written as:

$$
    G_t^{(R+I)} = G_t^{(R)} - \alpha\Phi(S_{k-1}),
$$

so the shaping term adds a **trajectory-dependent constant** that does *not* change the relative advantages within that rollout. PBRS invariance therefore holds **per trajectory**.
    
When we refresh, we copy the current policy into the teacher and use the new $\Phi$ only for **future** trajectories. This behaves like periodically updating a **baseline between batches**: it shifts the overall scale of returns across batches, but does not alter the within-trajectory ordering that drives policy improvement.

We refresh because TIPS relies on **alignment between teacher and policy distributions**. If the teacher is never updated, it becomes increasingly stale as the policy improves, and changes in $\Phi$ no longer reliably track what is useful for the current policy. If we refresh too frequently, $\Phi$ changes very rapidly and the baseline moves often, which mainly affects the **critic’s stability** rather than the underlying PBRS property.

To study this trade-off, we ablate the refresh interval (N $\in$ {1, 100, 200, 250, 500}) for Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3-4B in the **Refresh interval** of Sec. 4.3:

- Very rare refreshes ((N{=}500), effectively a fixed teacher) yield noticeably lower EM.
- There is a broad optimum around (N $\approx$ 200): Qwen2.5-7B reaches (41.7) EM and Qwen3-4B reaches (48.4) EM.
- Across the full range of moderate intervals ((100)–(500)), all TIPS runs still outperform PPO, indicating that TIPS does *not* rely on a finely tuned refresh rate.
[Screenshots of Fixed v.s. Refresh interval ablation](https://imgur.com/a/Z7zs3bo)

Empirically, we do observe a **small change in mean reward scale** ([W&B Plot](https://imgur.com/a/N4YkRkl)) right after refresh caused by the change of information reward scale, but **the critic loss ([W&B Plot](https://imgur.com/a/KQHm5c5)) and gradient norms ([W&B Plot](https://imgur.com/a/g9u3vCS)) remain stable and quickly re-equilibrate.** We only observe a **slight shift in the critic values** ([W&B Plot](https://imgur.com/a/lF38GyO)); critic training remains stable. And we do not see refresh-induced divergence or collapses.

We have added this discussion, the refresh-interval ablation, and the corresponding plots in the **Refresh interval** of Sec. 4.3 in the revised manuscript.


-----

**Q4**: Failure Modes: The advantage distribution (Fig. 5) for TIPS is much cleaner than PPO's. However, are there specific types of tasks or reasoning steps where the information-gain reward might provide misleading guidance (e.g., when new evidence is subtly distracting but doesn't immediately lower the teacher's likelihood)? Can you provide an example of a failure case for TIPS?

**A4**: We agree that characterizing failure modes for TIPS is important. The most common failure case we observe is when the base model already knows the answer to the question from pre-training, and a tool use only distracts the model. In this scenario, we often find negative rewards assigned to perfectly good tool calls. However, we found that the magnitude of these rewards are usually small compared to the outcome reward, and don’t appear to actively harm training. We have provided an example of this in Appendix G.2, Figure 12 ([screenshot](https://imgur.com/a/6M8xfUz)).

-----

We believe that our response and additional experiment results address your concerns. However, please do not hesitate to let us know if you have any additional comments.

summary.value: This paper introduces Turn-Level Information-Potential Reward Shaping (TIPS), a novel reinforcement learning framework designed to address the challenge of sparse rewards and difficult credit assignment in multi-turn, search-augmented LLMs. The proposed approach exploits the notion of "information gain" as an increase of the teacher model's log-likelihood of the correct answer. The gain in the form of log-likelihood ratio serves as Potential-Based Reward Shape (PBRS), which maintains policy invariance. The proposed approach follows a standard PPO training procedure. Experimental results on various QA tasks show that the proposed approach outperforms the comparison approach based on accuracy and training stability.

strengths.value:
1.	Modeling the "information gain" as a turn-level reward is intuitive, well-designed. It effectively addresses the critical problem of sparse credit assignment in long-horizon reasoning tasks.
2.	The authors provide detailed proof of policy invariance in Appendix C, which lends strong theoretical credentials to the statement that the approach used by them has not affected the original policy.
3.	Extensive experiments on several QA benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

weaknesses.value:
1.	Lack of efficiency analysis. TIPS requires two forward passes of the teacher model per turn (to compute the likelihood before and after the observation) for every rollout. This introduces a non-trivial computational cost compared to outcome-only methods.
2.	Have you considered using a distilled, smaller model as the teacher to minimize the computational overhead?  Besides, could the "information gain" signal be approximated in a more computationally efficient manner?
3.	The reward shaping heavily relies on a set of acceptable answers A to calculate the teacher's likelihood L(S;A). The performance might be sensitive to the completeness and quality of this answer set, especially for questions with many valid paraphrases. The robustness of TIPS on imperfect answer set hasn’t been investigated in the paper.
4.	The teacher model is the key component of TIPS, but its selection and properties are not deeply explored. The paper uses the same LLM as the backbones of  both the policy model and teacher model. It is unclear how the method could perform with a teacher of different capabilities (e.g., larger, smaller, or from a different family) or if the policy and teacher drift too far apart even with periodic refreshes.
5.	The authors only compare TIPS against naive RL baselines (PPO, GRPO) and their multi-turn extensions. Several key and highly relevant baselines [1-10] are missing from the main results table (Table 1), which makes it difficult to assess the true contribution of TIPS.

[1] Search-R1: Training LLMs to Reason and Leverage Search Engines with Reinforcement Learning.
[2] ReSearch: Learning to Reason with Search for LLMs via Reinforcement Learning.
[3] ReTool: Reinforcement Learning for Strategic Tool Use in LLMs.
[4] Beyond Ten Turns: Unlocking Long-Horizon Agentic Search with Large-Scale Asynchronous RL.
[5] Stop summation: Min-form credit assignment is all process reward model needs for reasoning.
[6] DeepRAG: Thinking to Retrieve Step by Step for Large Language Models.
[7] Deepdive: Advancing deep search agents with knowledge graphs and multi-turn rl.
[8] O-Searcher: A Searching-based Agent Model for Open-Domain Open-Ended Question Answering.
[9] Search-o1: Agentic Search-Enhanced Large Reasoning Models.
[10] R1-searcher: Incentivizing the search capability in llms via reinforcement learning.
[11] From <Answer> to <Think>: Multidimensional Supervision of Reasoning Process for LLM Optimization.
[12] Openprm: Building open-domain process-based reward models with preference trees.

6.	Experiments are restricted to the Qwen2.5 family. The performance and stability of TIPS haven’t been unverified on other model architectures (e.g., Llama, Deepseek) and a wider range of model scales, raising concerns about its general applicability.
7.	The author claims that they used the same experiment setting as used in Search-R1. However, the reported results in Table 1 are inconsistent with those in the cited Search-R1 paper. 
8.	Marginal Gains vs. High Cost: The performance gain is rather marginal, particularly in the case of the 3B model where it occasionally performs worse than baselines. With the added complexity and computational cost of the teacher model so high, the cost-benefit ratio does not seem favorable.

summary.value: This paper introduces TIPS (Turn-Level Information-Potential Reward Shaping), a novel method to address the sparse reward and credit assignment problem in training multi-turn, search-augmented Large Language Models (LLMs). The core idea is to provide dense, turn-level rewards by measuring the increase in the likelihood of a correct answer, as evaluated by a "teacher" model, after each reasoning-and-retrieval turn. This information-gain signal is framed as a Potential-Based Reward Shape (PBRS), which theoretically preserves policy invariance. The authors integrate TIPS into the PPO framework and evaluate it on seven open-domain QA benchmarks. Results show that TIPS consistently outperforms strong baselines like PPO and GRPO, achieving significant improvements in Exact Match and F1 scores (e.g., +11.8% EM and +13.6% F1 for a 7B model) while demonstrating superior training stability and more effective credit assignment.

strengths.value:
Originality: The core idea of using a teacher model's likelihood of the correct answer to compute information-gain rewards is highly original. It provides a principled and automated way to generate dense supervision, distinct from heuristic rules or learned reward models.

Quality: The work is of very high quality. The combination of a solid theoretical grounding (PBRS) with extensive and carefully designed empirical validation is commendable. The ablations and analysis sections are particularly thorough.

Clarity: The paper is a model of clarity. The writing is precise, the concepts are well-motivated, and the flow from problem statement to solution to validation is logical and easy to follow.

Significance: This work addresses a fundamental bottleneck in RLHF/RLVR for complex LLM tasks. The demonstrated improvements in performance and, crucially, in training stability, represent a significant advance. The method has the potential to become a standard component in the toolkit for training reasoning agents.

weaknesses.value:
The weaknesses are minor and do not detract from the overall excellent contribution.

1. Computational Overhead: While not explicitly quantified, using a teacher model (especially a 7B model) to compute log-likelihoods for every turn during training introduces non-trivial computational overhead compared to outcome-only rewards. A brief discussion of this cost (e.g., estimated % increase in training time or FLOPs) would be helpful for practitioners.

2. Teacher-Student Capacity: The method assumes the teacher model is sufficiently powerful to make reliable judgments about information gain. The paper uses the agent's own initial checkpoint as the teacher. It is unclear how the method would perform if the agent significantly diverges from the teacher's knowledge distribution, or if a less capable teacher were used. An ablation with teachers of different capacities could further strengthen the work.

3. Comparison to PRMs: The introduction contrasts TIPS with Process Reward Models (PRMs) by citing their need for "high-quality supervisory labels." However, recent work has explored training PRMs on synthetic or LLM-generated step-level feedback. A more direct comparison or discussion on how TIPS's "information gain" reward compares in quality and efficiency to a learned PRM would be insightful.

It is worth noting that I am not an expert in this field, and I will adjust my score based on the scores of other reviewers.

4. TIPS consistently outperforms all PPO and GRPO-based baselines across seven diverse QA benchmarks, using both 3B and 7B models. The performance gains are particularly pronounced on difficult multi-hop and out-of-domain (OOD) tasks, which is precisely where one would expect a better credit assignment method to excel.

3. The entire framework's success hinges on the availability and quality of a "teacher model". **A1:** We agree that quantifying the extra cost is important, and we have **added an Overhead Analysis section (App. H) with both FLOPs and wall-clock measurements.**

Using the FLOPs accounting from the VeRL codebase (including the extra teacher forward passes with KV-prefix caching), we find that TIPS increases the training FLOPs by only about **11–12%** over vanilla PPO across all tested backbones:

| Model | EM (Δ vs PPO) | F1 (Δ vs PPO) | FLOPs overhead |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct | 33.6 (+11.4%) | 41.1 (+10.2%) | 11.76% |
| Qwen3-4B-Instruct | 48.4 (+7.3%) | 57.1 (+6.1%) | 11.85% |
| Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct | 41.7 (+11.9%) | 51.2 (+13.7%) | 11.81% |
| Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct | 45.4 (+12.7%) | 53.1 (+10.6%) | 11.81% |
| LLaMA3.1-8B | 40.3 (+34.0%) | 49.0 (+29.3%) | 11.66% |

For wall-clock time, rollout generation dominates, so per-step runtime is largely driven by the policy’s average response length. To isolate the fixed overhead from teacher scoring, we measure the per-step time with reward computation on vs. off within the same TIPS run:

| Model | Without reward (s/step) | With reward (s/step) | Overhead (%) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen2.5-3B | 30.56 | 35.95 | 17.64 |
| Qwen2.5-7B | 93.00 | 108.22 | 16.37 |

Thus, teacher scoring adds roughly **11–12% training FLOPs** and **16–17% per-step wall-clock time**, with **no additional inference cost** (the teacher is not used at inference).

Given that TIPS yields **7–14% relative EM/F1 gains** on the Qwen family and **29–34% relative EM/F1 gains** on LLaMA3.1-8B, together with substantially improved training stability and reduced collapse rates, we believe this is a favorable cost–benefit trade-off.

---

**W2/Q2**: Teacher–student capacity and teacher selection: The method assumes the teacher is sufficiently powerful and uses the agent’s own initial checkpoint as teacher. How does TIPS behave if the policy diverges from the teacher, or if the teacher is weaker/stronger? An ablation over teacher capacities would help.

**A2.** TIPS does **not** require the teacher to be strictly stronger than the policy, nor to make “objectively correct” judgments. The key requirement is that the teacher’s distribution is **well aligned** with the policy’s distribution so that the teacher’s log-likelihoods over valid answers can act as a stable potential function.

In all main experiments we therefore choose the teacher to be a **frozen copy of the policy**, refreshed periodically. This guarantees availability at any scale (no extra model to train) and keeps the teacher and policy close in behavior.

To directly address the reviewer’s question, we also ran an ablation where we fix the policy and vary the teacher:

- **Frozen policy (self-teacher)** — our default;
- **Qwen3-4B-TIPS** — a stronger, TIPS-trained model;
- **LLaMA3.1-8B** — a cross-family model.

The EM results on the multi-turn QA suite are:

| Policy / Teacher | Frozen policy | Qwen3-4B-TIPS | LLaMA3.1-8B |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen2.5-7B | 41.7 (+11.9%) | 30 (−19.5%) | 29 (−22.2%) |
| Qwen3-4B | 48.4 (+7.3%) | 45.88 (+1.7%) | 43 (−4.7%) |

Using a **frozen copy of the policy** as teacher consistently performs best. Even a stronger TIPS-trained Qwen3-4B teacher underperforms the self-teacher, and a cross-family LLaMA teacher degrades performance further. This supports our design choice: for TIPS, **behavioral similarity between teacher and policy is more important than raw teacher capacity**.

We have added this ablation and a brief discussion of  **Teacher selection** to Section 4.3 of the revised manuscript. ([screenshot](https://imgur.com/a/6rclzlc)).

    These works focus on richer agent architectures and infrastructure (different tool setups, KG-based environments, asynchronous rollouts, closed-weight backbones, etc.) and often operate in different environments from ours. - **Process reward models (PRMs) \([5,11,12]\).**

summary.value:
This paper presents TIPS (Turn-level Information-Potential Shaping), a reinforcement learning framework for optimizing search-augmented large language models in open-domain question answering. The authors identify that existing reinforcement learning methods such as PPO and GRPO depend heavily on sparse, outcome-only rewards that are only provided at the end of an episode. This design makes it difficult to assign credit accurately across multiple reasoning and retrieval steps, leading to unstable learning dynamics.

TIPS addresses this limitation by introducing a turn-level dense reward mechanism. Instead of waiting for a final correctness signal, the framework measures how much each reasoning-and-retrieval step increases the teacher model’s confidence in the correct answer. This reward, based on the change in the teacher’s confidence, follows the Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS) principle, which guarantees that the underlying task objective remains unchanged while providing richer learning feedback. The system therefore offers fine-grained credit assignment across reasoning turns without compromising theoretical soundness.

The authors evaluate TIPS on seven open-domain QA benchmarks (including NQ, TriviaQA, 2Wiki, MuSiQue, and HotpotQA) using Qwen-2.5 models of 3B and 7B parameters. Across tasks, TIPS consistently surpasses PPO and GRPO in both accuracy and stability, with particularly strong improvements on multi-hop reasoning datasets.

strengths.value:
- Built on potential-based reward shaping, TIPS ensures that policy invariance is maintained while providing denser feedback signals, addressing a fundamental limitation in sparse-reward reinforcement learning for language models.
- The paper presents a well-structured pipeline—multi-turn reasoning, retrieval, teacher evaluation, and potential-based shaping—supported by consistent mathematical logic and implementation clarity.
- Evaluations across seven QA benchmarks and two model scales demonstrate reproducible and significant improvements in EM/F1 metrics, convergence speed, and training stability.
- The inclusion of advantage-distribution analysis and ablation studies on shaping coefficients and teacher refresh strategies provides concrete evidence of behavioral differences and system robustness.
- The framework is directly applicable to retrieval-augmented and reasoning-intensive LLMs, making it relevant for real-world agentic settings that require iterative tool use.

weaknesses.value:
- The reward signal is fully determined by the teacher model’s likelihood estimates. If the teacher is miscalibrated or biased, the shaping signal may misrepresent information gain. No calibration analysis or correction mechanism is discussed.
- All experiments use the same teacher model (Qwen-2.5), differing only in whether it is fixed or periodically refreshed. The paper does not evaluate how the reward behaves with different teachers, leaving the robustness of TIPS to teacher variation untested.
- The need to query the teacher model for every reasoning turn increases training cost compared to standard PPO/GRPO. The paper does not quantify the additional compute or discuss trade-offs between stability and efficiency.
- All results are reported using EM/F1 metrics. There is no qualitative or human study to determine whether TIPS improves reasoning coherence, interpretability, or factual correctness in practice.

**W3**: Comparison to PRMs: The introduction contrasts TIPS with Process Reward Models (PRMs) by citing their need for "high-quality supervisory labels." However, recent work has explored training PRMs on synthetic or LLM-generated step-level feedback. A more direct comparison or discussion on how TIPS's "information gain" reward compares in quality and efficiency to a learned PRM would be insightful.

**Response:** Thank you for pointing this out. Our intention in the introduction was not to claim that PRMs are infeasible, but to highlight a complementary design point: TIPS aims to provide a very low-cost, plug-in reward shaping signal, whereas PRMs require training an additional model from step-level supervision (human, synthetic, or LLM-generated).

Concretely, a fair experimental comparison to PRMs in our setting would require (i) generating or collecting step-level labels for multi-turn web-search traces, (ii) training a separate process reward model on this data, and (iii) running RL with an extra PRM forward pass at each step, on top of the existing verifier calls. To the best of our knowledge, there is currently no off-the-shelf PRM or any relevant dataset for our multi-turn QA / RLVR environment, and building such a pipeline would be a substantial project on its own, orthogonal to the core contribution of this paper.

By contrast, TIPS reuses a frozen copy of the policy as the “teacher” and leverages only existing outcome rewards; it introduces no additional training phase and adds a **relatively small runtime overhead (≈11–12% FLOPs, see Appendix. H).** Our goal is to show that this  **simple information-gain–based shaping already yields finer credit assignment** and more stable RL over PPO/GRPO.
